title: Sparsentan as First-Line Treatment in IgAN From SPARTAN.
abstract: The PROTECT trial demonstrated that sparsentan reduces proteinuria and preserves kidney function in patients with IgA nephropathy (IgAN). However, its potential as first-line therapy requires further investigation. SPARTAN (NCT04663204) is an experimental study evaluating efficacy, safety, and mechanistic actions of sparsentan in incident patients with IgAN. We present findings from a prespecified 24-week interim analysis. A total of 12 adults with incident biopsy-proven IgAN, urine protein excretion (UPE) ≥ 0.5 g/d, estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) ≥ 30 ml/min per 1.73 m2, and no renin-angiotensin system inhibitor (RASi) treatment within the previous 12 months were enrolled. Sparsentan was administered for 110 weeks with a 4-week safety follow-up. Assessments included proteinuria, eGFR, blood pressure (BP), body weight, total body water, cardiovascular measures, urinary biomarkers, and safety. Mean age was 35.8 years, median (interquartile range [IQR]) UPE was 1.7 (0.6-3.3) g/d, and mean eGFR was 70.2 (SD: 25.0) ml/min per 1.73 m2 at baseline. Urine protein-to-creatinine ratio (UPCR) declined rapidly (-61.9% at week 4), and reductions were sustained over 24 weeks (-68.8%); 58% of patients achieved complete remission of proteinuria (<0.3 g/d) during treatment. After an initial decrease, BP remained stable with stable eGFR, body weight, and cardiovascular risk variables. Total body water decreased. Rapid and sustained reductions in urinary biomarkers of inflammation, immune cell recruitment and modulation, and fibrosis were observed. The most frequent adverse event was dizziness (50% patients); 1 patient discontinued because of hypotension. First-line sparsentan reduced proteinuria by approximately 70% over 24 weeks and was generally well tolerated. Biomarker observations support anti-inflammatory and antifibrotic effects of sparsentan beyond its hemodynamic effects.

title: Bridging the Gap in Headache Care: Insights From the International Headache Society Survey in Nepal.
abstract: Headache disorders impose a substantial public health burden worldwide, with low- and middle-income countries like Nepal facing pronounced challenges due to limited healthcare infrastructure, inadequate provider training, and restricted access to essential treatments. This study aimed to assess the current state of headache care in Nepal, focusing on the distribution and training of healthcare providers, access to medications, and socioeconomic factors that affect treatment adherence. A cross-sectional survey was conducted as part of a multinational joint initiative by the International Headache Society and Middle East, North Africa and Asia Headache Group. Data were collected from 232 healthcare providers across Nepal using a survey questionnaire. Descriptive and comparative analyses assessed geographic disparities, medication accessibility, and provider preparedness. Most healthcare providers were concentrated in urban centers, with 80.2% reporting some form of training in headache care. However, training gaps persisted among rural and non-specialist providers. Overall, 72.0% of healthcare providers reported that their patients had to pay to access medications, while the median provider-estimated proportion of patients unable to afford medications was 40.0% (20.0%-60.0%). Access to migraine-specific therapies, such as triptans, topiramate, and amitriptyline, was substantially lower in rural areas. Providers in urban settings reported greater medication access and specialized care, while rural providers more frequently served younger, socioeconomically disadvantaged populations with limited treatment options. This study highlights significant disparities in headache care delivery in Nepal, driven by geographic, economic, and educational barriers. Furthermore, financial and geographic barriers to effective headache treatment raise important concerns regarding health equity and patients' rights to appropriate relief from avoidable pain and disability. To bridge these gaps, national policies should prioritize structured headache training, ensure essential headache medications are included in public formularies, and deploy telemedicine-based models in underserved regions.

title: Cerebral Small Vessel Disease and Its Associations with Cognitive Impairment, Gait Disturbance, and Europsychiatric Symptoms: A Narrative Review.
abstract: Cerebral small vessel disease (CSVD) encompasses a heterogeneous group of pathological processes affecting the small arteries, arterioles, capillaries, and venules of the brain. Beyond its well-recognized role in lacunar stroke and intracerebral hemorrhage, CSVD is increasingly understood as a major contributor to cognitive decline, gait impairment, and mood disturbances in older adults. These non-stroke manifestations often coexist and share common pathophysiological substrates, including endothelial dysfunction, blood-brain barrier disruption, chronic hypoperfusion, neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, and disruption of structural and functional brain networks. This narrative review synthesizes current evidence on the epidemiology, neuroimaging markers, and pathophysiological mechanisms of CSVD, with particular attention to its associations with cognitive impairment (predominantly executive dysfunction and slowed processing speed), gait abnormalities (reduced walking speed, increased stride variability, and elevated fall risk), and europsychiatric symptoms (vascular depression, apathy, and anxiety). The interactive relationships among these clinical phenotypes and the amplifying effects of comorbidities such as diabetes are also discussed. Finally, we review existing intervention strategies, particularly blood pressure control, and highlight emerging therapeutic targets and unresolved questions that warrant further investigation.

title: Adapted Massed Exposure Therapy Enhanced with MDMA for PTSD (aMETEMP): A randomized, double-masked protocol adapted for Veterans Affairs healthcare system.
abstract: Posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) remains prevalent and disabling, especially among veterans, with a substantial proportion failing to achieve remission following first-line evidence-based trauma-focused psychotherapies. 3,4-Methylenedioxymethamphetamine (MDMA) is hypothesized to enhance psychotherapy outcomes through effects on fear extinction, cognitive flexibility, and emotional engagement, and is being studied as a promising augmentation strategy for PTSD psychotherapy. There is limited research combining MDMA with evidence-based PTSD treatment. MDMA-assisted psychotherapy trials to date have also been limited by lack of an active comparator and functional unmasking. We describe the methodology of an ongoing randomized, double-masked, pilot trial evaluating massed prolonged exposure (PE) therapy enhanced with MDMA for PTSD (aMETEMP), adapted for a U.S. Veterans Affairs outpatient setting. Up to 20 veterans with PTSD in the VA will receive a 6-8hr in-person MDMA dosing session (randomized dose 35 mg - 125 mg) integrated with a 3-week massed exposure protocol. The remaining visits are virtual and include PE sessions and sessions to prepare for and process the MDMA session (28-30hrs total over 11 visits), with the use of telehealth intended to improve access and ease patient burden. After treating the first 4 participants, who were fully informed of the trial design, we switched to using an incomplete disclosure strategy (not disclosing the number of treatment arms or specific possible doses) to further improve masking. Primary outcomes include PTSD severity using the Clinician-Administered PTSD Scale for DSM-5, safety, feasibility, and masking success. Findings are intended to provide preliminary descriptive information regarding feasibility, safety/tolerability, masking integrity, and symptom-change signals for aMETEMP with incomplete disclosure in a large outpatient healthcare system. NCT06117306.

title: An effective screening tool for uncovering degenerative cervical myelopathy: Results of the prospective multicenter SCREEN-DCM study.
abstract: Degenerative cervical myelopathy (DCM) is a leading cause of spinal cord injury, yet it remains frequently undiagnosed. Earlier identification may help guide patients into appropriate diagnostic and referral pathways before substantial neurological disability has accumulated. This study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic performance of SCREEN-DCM for identifying previously undiagnosed DCM. We conducted a prospective multicenter diagnostic accuracy study, where 200 consecutive adults presenting with lumbar degenerative disease were screened with the SCREEN-DCM clinical score, based on established DCM symptoms, signs, and risk factors. SCREEN-DCM scores ≥3 were considered positive. 69 (34.5%) participants screened positive and 131 (65.5%) screened negative. Cervical MRI was performed in 83 participants. DCM was identified in 29 of 57 screen-positive patients and 1 of 26 screen-negative patients. SCREEN-DCM demonstrated 96.7% sensitivity, 47.2% specificity, 50.9% positive predictive value, 96.2% negative predictive value, and an AUC of 0.87 (95% CI, 0.79-0.95). Approximately two MRIs were required to detect one DCM case among screen-positive patients. Diagnostic sensitivity remained high across exploratory age groups. A simplified eight-variable model showed comparable discrimination (AUC, 0.85; 95% CI, 0.77-0.93), with Hoffman's sign, gait ataxia, and hand clumsiness among the strongest predictors of DCM. SCREEN-DCM has a very high sensitivity to identify DCM in previously undiagnosed patients. By identifying patients who may otherwise experience diagnostic delay, the screening tool could support earlier referral and prevention of avoidable neurological disability.

title: Hybrid Liposome-U87MG Membrane Nanovesicles Enhance Brain Delivery and Therapeutic Efficacy of Irinotecan in Orthotopic Glioma.
abstract: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) and hydrolytic inactivation of the lactone form limit the efficacy of irinotecan (CPT-11) against glioma. To address these challenges, we developed a CPT-11-loaded hybrid liposome-U87MG cell membrane nanovesicle formulation (Hybrid/CPT-11), an underexplored biomimetic strategy for glioma therapy. This formulation combines the drug-loading and stabilizing capacity of liposomes (Lip) with the membrane-derived functionality of biomimetic nanovesicles (BNVs) prepared from U87MG cell membranes. Three preparation strategies-co-incubation, freeze-thaw followed by co-extrusion, and film hydration followed by co-extrusion-were compared. Membrane fusion was assessed by Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET) to select the optimal process. Physicochemical properties (TEM, hydrodynamic size/PDI, encapsulation efficiency, short-term storage and serum stability) were characterized. In vitro performance (U87MG uptake, 3D spheroid penetration, proliferation and migration inhibition) and in vivo biodistribution (Cy5 imaging), antitumor efficacy (bioluminescence imaging, tumor burden, survival), and biosafety (body weight, hematology, major-organ histology) were evaluated in orthotopic U87MG and U87MG-Luc glioma models. Freeze-thaw followed by co-extrusion yielded the greatest FRET decrease and was selected. Hybrid/CPT-11 exhibited a uniform nanoscale size (178.4 ± 4.6 nm, PDI 0.22 ± 0.01), high encapsulation efficiency (61.6%), and stability. In vitro, Hybrid/Cou-6 showed enhanced cellular uptake and deeper penetration in 3D spheroids versus free Cou-6 and BNV/Cou-6. Hybrid/CPT-11 also exhibited the lowest IC50 in U87MG cells compared with free CPT-11 and nonhybrid controls. In vivo, Hybrid/Cy5 prolonged systemic signal and enhanced brain accumulation versus Lip/Cy5 and BNV/Cy5. In orthotopic U87MG-Luc glioma, Hybrid/CPT-11 suppressed tumor bioluminescence, reduced endpoint tumor burden, and extended median survival (21 vs 16 days for free CPT-11), without significant weight loss, hematologic abnormalities, or major-organ pathology. This study developed a FRET-optimized hybrid liposome-U87MG cell membrane nanovesicle formulation that enhances brain delivery and therapeutic efficacy of irinotecan in orthotopic glioma.

title: Pomegranate Seed Oil Biologically Engineered Lactobacillus Extracellular Vesicles with Enhanced Yield and Brain Delivery via ApoE-Enriched Protein Corona.
abstract: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) is a major bottleneck for nanomedicine-based treatment of central nervous system (CNS) disorders. Lactobacillus-derived extracellular vesicles (LEV) are promising biocompatible nanocarriers, but their low production yield and limited BBB permeability hinder their development. We hypothesized that stimulation of Lactobacillus with pomegranate seed oil (PSO), or its nanoemulsion (PSO NE), could remodel the LEV membrane to simultaneously enhance vesicle production and brain accumulation. Lactobacillus was stimulated with PSO or PSO NE to generate engineered LEV. Lipidomic and proteomic analyses were performed to characterize membrane remodeling and plasma protein corona formation. Oleuropein (OL) was loaded into different LEV formulations, and their BBB permeability and brain accumulation were evaluated in vivo. The anti-amyloid β (Aβ) aggregation activity and biocompatibility of the engineered LEVs were also assessed. PSO and PSO NE increased LEV production by approximately 3- and 5-fold, respectively, while markedly remodeling their membrane composition, with enrichment of phospholipids, triglycerides, and apolipoproteins. Upon exposure to plasma, the remodeled LEVs spontaneously acquired an apolipoprotein E (ApoE)-rich protein corona, facilitating BBB transport through low-density lipoprotein receptor (LDLR)-mediated transcytosis. Accordingly, OL-loaded LEV-PSO and LEV-PSO NE achieved 5-7-fold higher brain exposure than free OL, compared with only a 1.17-fold increase for conventional OL@LEV. Both native and OL-loaded LEVs inhibited Aβ aggregation, with OL-loaded formulations showing stronger activity. Repeated administration for 14 days demonstrated good biocompatibility and significantly increased BBB LDLR expression following LEV-PSO and LEV-PSO NE treatment. PSO-mediated membrane engineering substantially improves LEV production and BBB transport through protein-corona modulation, providing a scalable and versatile platform for CNS drug delivery.

title: Eigenmode decomposition of asymmetries in whole-brain effective connectivity reveals multiscale hierarchical dynamics.
abstract: The human brain is a complex system operating far from equilibrium, yet how whole-brain directed hierarchical patterns emerge across spatiotemporal scales remains unclear. While functional and structural hierarchies have been described, no framework has exhaustively integrated a node-level hierarchical ranking of directed brain networks with non-equilibrium dynamics decomposition across spectral scales. Here we isolate the irreversible rotational component of whole-brain effective connectivity (EC), encoding the hierarchical network derived from antisymmetric interactions, and decompose it into EC eigenmodes across spectral ranges. Hierarchy strengthens near criticality, where slow oscillatory modes dominate and reflects long-range anatomical scaffolding of whole-brain activity. Our decomposition provides the first EC eigenmode-based multiscale representation of temporal irreversibility, revealing dual counterpropagating streams along the unimodal-transmodal axis at distinct frequencies and identifying slow-mode individual-specific signatures, with unimodal networks contributing disproportionately to subject identifiability. Altogether, this work provides a unified EC-based framework for characterizing whole-brain hierarchical patterns across spectral scales and individuals.

title: Bulk RNA sequencing dataset of hippocampi from RORγt transgenic mice and wild type littermates.
abstract: This dataset comprises bulk RNA-sequencing data from bilateral hippocampi of six untreated, 10-week-old male mice: three heterozygous RORγt-transgenic mice and three wild-type littermates on a C57BL/6 background. Total RNA was extracted using TRIzol, and RNA integrity numbers ranged from 8.1 to 8.6. Ribosomal RNA-depleted, directional libraries were prepared from 500 ng of RNA per sample and sequenced on an Illumina NextSeq 500 with a 2 × 36-bp paired-end configuration. The received reads were 35 or 36 bases long. The 48 original compressed FASTQ files were consolidated into 12 files, preserving 83,357,563 read pairs and their pairing. Original mm10 count and RPKM matrices each contain 49,585 feature entries. An additional GRCm39 reanalysis using Ensembl release 116 provides gene-level fragment counts for 78,348 annotated features, coordinate-sorted alignments and sample-level exploratory analyses. FastQC and MultiQC reports describe raw-read quality, and principal component analysis summarizes variation across all six samples. Original sequencing data and expression matrices are deposited in NCBI Gene Expression Omnibus under accession GSE347403.

title: Early life threat and caregiver-related fear learning in early childhood.
abstract: Across species, caregivers regulate offspring fear learning and expression of conditioned fear responses. Rodent studies additionally demonstrate that pups exposed to rough maternal care show disruptions in this adaptive learning mechanism. An analogous experience, early life threat (i.e., interpersonal violence), is strongly associated with developmental outcomes in children. However, we do not understand the extent to which early life threat is associated with fear learning in the context of caregivers in children, although this may be an important mechanism shaping development. The present study utilized data from 219 children who completed a novel fear learning paradigm, in which conditioned fear responses to caregivers and strangers were measured using skin conductance responses. First, we show that children show differential skin conductance responses to stranger stimuli, but not to caregiver stimuli. Second, we find subtle associations between early life threat and conditioned fear responses to caregiver stimuli. Specifically, early life threat was associated with small increases in skin conductance responses to the caregiver-safety cue compared to the caregiver-threat cue. These data show similarities with the rodent literature and identify a potential mechanism by which early life threat may shape child development.

title: Diagnostic Accuracy of the Three-Gene Host-Response Test in Blood for Tuberculosis: A Systematic Review.
abstract: Molecular diagnostic tests and sputum-based assays are common techniques for the initial evaluation of tuberculosis (TB). However, given their limitations in certain clinical contexts, efforts have been made to develop other diagnostic markers. This review evaluated the diagnostic accuracy of a three-gene host-response test (TB score) for the diagnosis of TB. We performed systematic searches in seven databases until July 2026. We included observational studies evaluating the diagnostic accuracy of the TB score to diagnosis of TB across different clinical contexts. Risk of bias was assessed using QUADAS-2. Meta-analysis was performed using the logit function, and GRADE was employed to assess certainty of evidence (CoE). Twenty-eight studies were included. For distinguishing pulmonary TB from other respiratory diseases, the TB score showed a pooled sensitivity and specificity of 0.80 (95% CI: 0.73-0.84) and 0.72 (95% CI: 0.64-0.78), respectively, with an AUC of 0.82. When comparing pulmonary TB to healthy controls, sensitivity was 0.75 and specificity was 0.86, with an AUC of 0.87. Performance was lower for meningeal tuberculosis (sensitivity 0.58; specificity 0.67) and for distinguishing active from latent TB (sensitivity 0.73; specificity 0.76). Risk of bias was generally low. The CoE for most outcomes was very low. The TB score shows moderate diagnostic accuracy for pulmonary TB, with pooled sensitivity below the WHO TPP minimum for a standalone triage test. High heterogeneity and very low CoE limit confidence in these findings. Its potential role as a complementary tool remains investigational and requires validation in prospective studies.

title: A Human iPSC-Derived Neuron and Glioma Culture Model Reveals Increased Neuronal Excitability and Loss of GABAergic Inhibition.
abstract: Gliomas engage in bidirectional interactions with neural circuits, driving hyperexcitability, disruption of excitatory-inhibitory balance, and tumor-associated seizures. Human in vitro models that enable functional interrogation of tumor-induced changes in glutamatergic-GABAergic neuronal crosstalk remain limited. We established a defined human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived culture comprising of glutamatergic neurons, GABAergic neurons, and astrocytes with and without glioma cells. Network maturation and function were characterized using immunocytochemistry, multi-electrode array recordings, and whole-cell patch-clamp electrophysiology. Neuronal cultures developed mature synaptic architecture, spontaneous coordinated network activity, and suppression of neuronal firing following treatment with the GABA-A agonist muscimol, demonstrating functional GABAergic signaling. Glioma incorporation increased spike rate, increased coordinated network activity, and reversed the response to muscimol from suppression to elevation of neuronal firing, indicating disrupted GABAergic signaling. Whole-cell patch-clamp recordings demonstrated increased intrinsic excitability of glutamatergic neurons following glioma co-culture, characterized by increased action potential firing frequency and increased action potential amplitude. This human iPSC-derived glutamatergic-GABAergic neuron model recapitulates key features of tumor-induced neuronal dysfunction while enabling complementary network- and single-cell analyses. The model provides a relevant, scalable, and accessible system for mechanistic investigation of bidirectional neuron-glioma interactions and preclinical evaluation of therapies targeting tumor-induced neuronal dysfunction.

title: Brain Age Gap Progression in Individuals at Risk for Neurodegeneration.
abstract: Neuroimaging is a widely used modality for characterizing neurodegeneration in various health conditions. Brain age gap has emerged as a promising biomarker for monitoring brain health from neuroimaging data using machine learning algorithms. Recent studies have leveraged coVariance neural networks (VNN)-driven pipelines based on the advancements in graph signal processing for relatively transparent construction of brain age gap from neuroimaging data. In this paper, we focus on a longitudinal study of VNN-based brain age gap in conjunction with Alzheimer's Progression Score (APS) in individuals that are at a higher risk of neurodegeneration due to family history of Alzheimer's disease. APS is a multimodal marker of disease progression. The longitudinal analysis of APS and VNN-derived brain age gap metrics revealed that a higher risk of disease progression at baseline predicted a larger rate of increase in brain age gap in follow-up visits. Thus, our findings revealed potential stratification in the brain age gap modulated by clinical/biological risks of AD in the at-risk population.

title: Cellularized, needle-deployed intracortical arrays for brain electrophysiology.
abstract: Bioelectronic medicine enables direct interfacing with native cell populations but remains limited by poor long-term integration and minimal interaction with non-electroactive cells. In contrast, regenerative medicine promotes tissue integration yet lacks bidirectional functionality. Here, we present a hybrid implantation methodology combining a tissue engineered cellularized hydrogel with a neural recording array for simultaneous delivery into the brain via needle placement. This approach enables co-localized transplantation of cells and electronics while minimizing surgical footprint. Post-implantation electrophysiological recordings show functional integration with surrounding neural tissue, demonstrating the feasibility of this platform for coupled bioelectronic sensing and regenerative capabilities. The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1557/s43579-026-01033-7.

title: Beyond the blood-brain barrier: amivantamab plus lazertinib in EGFR-mutant non-small cell lung cancer with brain and leptomeningeal metastases.
Rewiring of adult neural networks - learning from structural plasticity across multiple scales.
abstract: Synaptic connections are continuously formed and eliminated even in adult neuronal networks. This process - called structural plasticity - allows networks to change their topology to learn and adapt to their environment or compensate for lesions. Yet, in contrast to synaptic plasticity, structural plasticity is less well studied and understood. We here present the current state of knowledge as well as open problems in the field along three guiding questions: (1) What regulates structural plasticity in biological neural networks? (2) What are the functional consequences and advantages of structural plasticity in adult neural networks? (3) How can our understanding of structural plasticity be translated into clinical and technological applications? We argue that understanding structural plasticity is a problem involving multiple temporal and spatial scales. Solving this problem thus requires collaborative efforts of experimentalists, theoreticians as well as computational modelers, and has the potential for comprehensive neuroscientific insights that can guide the development of medical applications, artificial neural networks as well as neuromorphic computing.

title: Immune modulation by lipopolysaccharide preconditioning: A novel approach to neuropathic pain in rats.
abstract: Neuropathic pain (NPP) resulting from peripheral nerve compression is associated with heightened nociceptive sensitivity and increased neuroinflammation. This study investigated the effects of lipopolysaccharide (LPS) preconditioning on behavioral and inflammatory outcomes in a rat model of the chronic constriction injury (CCI)-induced NPP. Animals were assigned to groups including Control, CCI (underwent CCI surgery), LPS (0.01 mg/kg) + CCI, LPS (0.1 mg/kg) + CCI, and LPS (0.5 mg/kg) + CCI, which received LPS intraperitoneally and then underwent CCI surgery. Pain-related behaviors were assessed using the Acetone Test and Hot Plate Test on days 7 and 14 after CCI induction. Then, Spinal cord samples were collected to quantify tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNFα) levels, a key pro-inflammatory mediator. CCI induction significantly increased hypersensitivity to pain, accompanied by elevated TNF-α expression in the spinal cord. LPS preconditioning attenuated pain behaviors and reduced TNF-α levels compared with the CCI group. These findings suggest that LPS preconditioning modulates neuroimmune responses and may confer protective effects against NPP development induced by peripheral nerve compression.

title: Syntaxin-1 and syntaxin binding protein 1-1 are required for planarian behavior and brain regeneration.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Nervous system regeneration requires creation of new neurons and their integration into new and existing networks. How new neurons find their targets and reconnect in the environment of regenerating tissue remains a major gap in knowledge. The planarian Schmidtea mediterranea is well suited to the study of neural regeneration due to the remarkable ability of planarians to regenerate their entire body, including the nervous system. However, we have not yet been able to explore synaptogenesis in regeneration using planarians due to a lack of tools to study synapses. Here we investigate potential players in planarian synapse, focusing on the conserved syntaxin protein family, which functions in neurotransmitter vesicle fusion at the synapse. We found that reduction of either syntaxin-1 ( stx1 ) or syntaxin-binding protein 1-1 ( stxbp1-1 ) decreased locomotion and impeded brain regeneration, specifically in synapse-rich regions. Our observations support STX-1 and STXBP1-1 as bona fide synapse components, providing a starting point for studies neuronal connectivity during homeostatic remodeling and regeneration.

title: Reverse engineering Lewy bodies suggests α-synuclein pathology as condensatopathy.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Understanding how soluble monomeric α-synuclein transitions into pathological α-synuclein (Lewy bodies) has remained a central challenge in neurodegeneration. Existing models, largely based on treating cells and animals with pre-formed α-synuclein fibrils cannot account for the emergence of the first inclusion without pre-existing seeds. Here, we combine in vitro reconstitutions, computational modeling and a minimal cellular system to show that phase separation of α-synuclein with an interacting scaffold can recapitulate Lewy body-like structures. An unbiased proteomics screen, live-cell imaging, correlative light-electron microscopy, and soft X-ray tomography show that Lewy body-like structures are associated with redistribution of actin and membrane-bound organelles, with mitochondria accumulating at their periphery in an actin-dependent manner. Structural analyses further indicate that α-synuclein condensates provide local environments in which the insoluble (-sheets can form. Together, these findings support a seed-independent trajectory from soluble α-synuclein through condensation and progressive immobilization to Lewy body-like assemblies and, subsequently, insoluble (-sheet fibrils. This framework offers a new mechanistic route for understanding the disease progression and promises to guide the design of innovative therapeutic interventions.

title: The role of the NLRP3 inflammasome in a CLN2 mouse model of neuroinflammation.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Neuronal ceroid lipofuscinoses, or Batten disease, comprises a group of inherited pediatric neurodegenerative disorders, and is characterized by the lysosomal accumulation of the fluorescent storage material lipofuscin. The human classical late-infantile form of the disorder (CLN2) is caused by mutations in the CLN2 / Tripeptidyl peptidase 1 ( TPP1 ) gene. Comparable to human CLN2, a knockout of the Tpp1 gene ( Tpp1 -/- ) in the mouse leads to progressive vision loss, ataxia, motor atrophy, seizures, and premature death. While we previously showed using bulk RNA-seq analysis that reactive gliosis develops between 3 and 4 months in this animal model, the role of the inflammasome in CLN2 remains unexplored. The inflammasome is a multiprotein complex formed through pattern recognition receptor engagement, which culminate in the cleavage and release of interleukin-1 beta. Here we report that while some inflammasome-associated genes are upregulated as early as 1-month in the Tpp1 -/- cerebellum, it is not until 3-months-old that all gene transcripts necessary for inflammasome assembly and function are upregulated, leading to IL1β release. In Tpp1 -/- slice cultures, we demonstrated that MCC950, an inhibitor of inflammasome assembly, downregulates transcriptional expression of genes associated with reactive microglia and inflammasome function. Furthermore, prophylactic administration of MCC950 in drinking water of Tpp1 -/- animals for two months is sufficient to lower the expression of these same genes in the forebrain and cerebellum, suggesting that inflammasome inhibitors are promising therapeutics for CLN2 and neurodegeneration broadly.

title: Braintree: An agentic framework for in-silico vision neuroscience.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Vision neuroscience has many of the ingredients needed to conduct experiments entirely in-silico. We need AI systems that can reason over scientific knowledge, generative methods for creating precisely controlled stimuli, image-computable models that can predict neural responses with increasing accuracy, and tools that can analyze and interpret data. Here we take the first step toward making a vision neuroscience experiment end-to-end computable. We introduce Braintree, an agentic framework that can autonomously run multi-experiment studies directly with in-silico models of human visual cortex. Given a hypothesis, Braintree can reason over the current literature, design an experiment, build a stimulus set from algorithmically manipulated or synthesized stimuli, run the experiment on candidate brain encoding models, analyze the responses and then use the results to design even stronger tests. The entire loop runs autonomously and can accept human input at any stage. We evaluated Braintree on three increasingly open-ended scientific problems. First, Braintree reproduced published findings using their original stimuli and then asked whether the same effects could be replicated with entirely new stimulus sets that it constructed. Second, it designed new experiments to find stimulus dimensions that could drive two brain regions differently, even when those regions otherwise had similar response profiles. Third, it searched for experiments that could tell competing models of the same brain region apart. Experiments discovered using just two models also exposed differences across a much broader set of models, suggesting that Braintree had found more general dimensions along which brain models disagree. Braintree can augment the capabilities of a vision neuroscientist as a verifier for existing hypotheses, a test-bed for new ideas, and/or a tool for generating stimuli that can discriminate between competing hypotheses or models of the brain. Braintree shows how AI agents and brain models can work together to make in-silico vision neuroscience experiment computable, allowing vision scientists to explore many more experiment conditions and identify the most informative ones to test on the human brain.

title: From Intrinsic Topography to Cognitive Prediction: Benchmarking Approaches to Personalized Cortical Parcellation.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Personalized functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) adapts cortical parcellations to individual functional anatomy. Various methods have been proposed that differ in how they combine group-level information, spatial constraints, and individual functional data. Using the Human Connectome Project Young Adult dataset ( N = 947), we compared five personalized parcellation methods and a standard group-level atlas. For each method, we calculated functional homogeneity, test-retest reliability, parcel contiguity, and inter-individual Dice overlap. Personalized parcellation methods generally yielded higher functional homogeneity and lower inter-individual Dice than the group atlas, while test-retest reliability of functional connectivity was high across methods. Parcel contiguity differed across methods: some approaches produced almost entirely contiguous parcels, whereas others frequently produced spatially disconnected components, indicating that the detection of candidate ectopic variants depends partly on the parcellation strategy. We also examined whether connectivity and topographic features were associated with and predicted general intelligence ( g ). Using structural equation modeling, intra-individual parcel size variability and inter-individual parcel size similarity derived from the hierarchical Bayesian method (gMSHBM) were positively associated with g , whereas no corresponding association survived correction for the other methods. Using kernel ridge regression, functional connectivity significantly predicted g , with the group atlas yielding the highest predictive accuracy, consistent with a potential advantage of cross-individual spatial correspondence for edge-wise prediction. Finally, we assessed robustness across four preprocessing pipelines. Although gMSHBM parcellations were not re-estimated, relative between-method patterns in several spatial characteristics were largely preserved. In contrast, brain-behavior associations involving time-series-derived features varied substantially with preprocessing, whereas parcel-size associations were more stable. We conclude that personalized parcellation approaches are associated with distinct trade-offs in spatial correspondence, topographic variability, and downstream predictive utility. The choice of parcellation strategy therefore affects both the properties of individualized maps and the brain-behavior information derived from them.

title: Dopamine Release from the Locus Coeruleus Enables Temporal Binding in the Hippocampus.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: The hippocampus forms memories by associating events that are separated in time. These associations can be studied using trace conditioning, a procedure where a temporal gap is inserted between a conditional stimulus and an unconditional stimulus. Here, we examined how dopaminergic projections to CA1 support trace fear conditioning. Using fiber photometry and genetic lesions, we demonstrate that locus coeruleus (LC)-derived dopamine, rather than VTA input, is the primary source of dopamine in CA1 and is essential for trace learning. LC lesions reduced CA1 principal neuron activity and c-Fos expression. In-vivo imaging revealed that successful learning requires post-shock reactivation of stimulus-specific ensembles, a process compromised by LC lesions or long trace intervals. Finally, optogenetic stimulation of LC-CA1 projections during the post-shock period was sufficient to rescue learning in long-trace protocols. These findings identify LC-CA1 dopamine as a critical regulator of temporal binding via the facilitation of hippocampal memory trace reactivation.

title: Turbulent dynamics and in silico perturbation-based measures are disrupted across biological stages of Alzheimers disease.
journal: medRxiv : the preprint server for health sciences
abstract: According to the AT(N) framework, Alzheimers disease (AD) can be biologically characterised by amyloid deposition, tau pathology, and neurodegeneration, yet how these processes relate to whole-brain dynamics remains unclear. Here, we investigated these relationships and the link between whole-brain dynamics and cognitive dysfunction using multimodal neuroimaging from 145 ADNI3 participants. We combined multiscale measures of turbulent dynamics with responses to in silico perturbations obtained from whole-brain models. AD progression was characterised by a scale-dependent reorganisation of turbulent dynamics where information flow showed the strongest contribution to the dynamics-related variance in cognitive performance. Large-scale turbulence was associated with all three AT(N) components. Model-based information capability and susceptibility measures progressively decreased across AD stages and were associated with amyloid burden and regional tau deposition. Model-free features discriminated comparisons involving AD dementia, whereas adding model-based measures produced modest, metric-dependent changes in classification performance. Exploratory analyses showed spatial alignment between large-scale turbulence alterations and AD-risk gene-expression gradients, with APOE among the strongest associations in both disease-stage contrasts examined. Lastly, we found a progressive decoupling between turbulent dynamics and the E:I balance across AD stages. Together, these findings link model-based and model-free measures of whole-brain dynamics to proteinopathy, neurodegeneration, and cognitive impairment, supporting their complementary value for characterising AD progression.

title: Therapeutic acute intermittent hypoxia does not alter whole-brain cerebrovascular function in healthy individuals.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Acute intermittent hypoxia (AIH) therapy is a promising intervention known to elicit beneficial neuroplasticity. It has been suggested that AIH may also modulate cerebrovascular function, yet the cerebrovascular effects of specific therapeutic intermittent hypoxia protocols remain poorly characterized. Understanding whether AIH results in favorable or adverse cerebrovascular changes is critical in establishing the safety of AIH treatments in populations with elevated cerebrovascular risk. This study investigated cerebral blood flow, cerebrovascular reactivity to hypoxia, and blood pressure effects in a sham-controlled crossover trial ( NCT05164705 ). Healthy young adults (n=18) completed three-week arms of AIH (12 sessions, 15 cycles of 60 seconds hypoxia alternated with 60 seconds normoxia) and sham (6 sessions, normoxia) treatments; phase-contrast and arterial spin labeling magnetic resonance imaging were used to quantify whole-brain and regional cerebral blood flow and hypoxic cerebrovascular reactivity. Blood pressure was measured acutely (before and after each intervention session) and longitudinally (before and after 3 weeks of treatment). AIH treatment did not significantly alter whole-brain resting cerebral blood flow or cerebrovascular reactivity to hypoxia. Blood pressure was unaffected by the treatment acutely or longitudinally. Voxel-wise analysis identified modest regional perfusion increases in the frontal pole, postcentral gyri, and precentral gyri with AIH relative to sham. Significant variability between subjects and between sessions in the hypoxic burden delivered with this AIH protocol was also identified. Overall, this three-week therapeutic AIH protocol produced minimal sustained hemodynamic changes in healthy young adults. The insights from this trial lay a foundation for safely expanding access to this promising rehabilitative intervention in clinical populations.

title: Breast Cancer-derived PDGFB Remodels the CNS Vascular Niche to Promote Brain, Spinal and Leptomeningeal Metastasis.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Central nervous system (CNS) metastases are a major driver of breast cancer (BC) mortality. Recently, our group demonstrated that platelet-derived growth factor-B (PDGFB) and its receptor, platelet-derived growth factor receptor-beta (PDGFRβ), promote BC metastasis to the brain; however, the cellular/molecular mechanisms driving this process remain unclear. Here, we investigated tumor-derived PDGFB effects on the CNS vascular niche in regulating metastatic spread. Triple-negative BC cells were engineered to overexpress PDGFB and used to evaluate endothelial sprouting, blood-brain barrier (BBB) function, vascular permeability and experimental CNS metastasis. A novel retro-orbital (RO) injection model was used to study leptomeningeal/spinal experimental metastasis. PDGFB enhanced human brain microvascular endothelial cell (HBMEC) sprouting, induced cell migration in BBB spheroids, increased permeability in 3D models, and disrupted tight junction proteins in HBMECs. Notably, alterations in vascular permeability were observed in both PDGFRβ-positive and PDGFRβ-negative endothelial systems, suggesting PDGFB can remodel the CNS vasculature through multiple mechanisms. In vivo , PDGFB increased CNS metastatic burden and altered tumor vasculature in xenograft and allograft models of BC. Furthermore, PDGFB promoted robust colonization of both spinal and leptomeningeal compartments, identifying a previously underappreciated role for this signaling pathway in a clinically devastating form of CNS metastasis. Analysis of patient transcriptomic datasets revealed enrichment of angiogenesis-related pathways in PDGFB-high tumors from patients who developed CNS metastases. Collectively, these findings identify tumor-derived PDGFB as a key regulator of CNS vascular remodeling and metastatic tropism, while introducing a new experimental framework to study spinal metastases and leptomeningeal disease in BC. Tumor-derived PDGFB remodels the CNS vasculature and disrupts barrier integrityPDGFB promotes brain, spinal, and leptomeningeal metastasisRetro-orbital injections provide a new model of leptomeningeal and spinal metastasis. Central nervous system (CNS) metastases are among the most lethal complications of breast cancer. Vascular cooption is recognized as a critical step in the metastatic cascade, but the tumor-derived signals which mediate this process are not fully understood. This study identifies PDGFB as a key signaling molecule which modulates the CNS endothelium, a previously underappreciated function. Beyond advancing our understanding of PDGFB-driven brain metastasis, this work also expands the role of PDGFB in promoting spinal and leptomeningeal metastasis. We establish a mechanistic framework connecting tumor-derived PDGFB to vascular dysfunction and CNS tropism, highlighting a potential opportunity to improve patient prognosis. Additionally, we employ a novel experimental model of leptomeningeal disease through retro-orbital (RO) injection of breast cancer cells. Together, these findings provide new insight into CNS metastasis while establishing experimental tools that may accelerate advancements in the understanding and treatment of brain, spinal, and leptomeningeal metastasis.

title: Intranasal L-MYC Neural Stem Cells Restore Neurovascular and Neuroimmune Homeostasis After TBI via CX3CL1 Upregulation and ICAM-1 Downregulation.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) triggers persistent neuroimmune and neurovascular dysfunction that contributes to secondary brain injury and limits recovery. Here, we investigated whether a single intranasal dose of LMNSC01 could reprogram post-traumatic neuroinflammatory and neurovascular responses and whether these effects were conserved across biological sex. Immunocompetent male and female rats underwent a controlled cortical impact (CCI) or Sham surgery and 7 days later received a single bolus dose of LMNSC01 (6 × 10 6 cells/dose) or vehicle. Integrated histological and transcriptomic analyses and multiplex tissue ELISA were used to characterize injury- and treatment-associated responses. CCI induced persistent but sex-dependent transcriptional changes. Male rats exhibited prominent innate immune, adhesion, extracellular matrix, and tissue remodeling responses, whereas females demonstrated broader activation of microglial, interferon, complement, MHC/antigen presentation, and humoral/adaptive immune pathways. LMNSC01 treatment reprogrammed these distinct injury states through partially sex-specific mechanisms. In males, LMNSC01 increased endogenous immune-regulatory mediators, including Il1rn , and reduced pathways associated with adhesion and immune-cell trafficking. In females, treatment decreased expression of genes related to microglial, leukocyte, MHC/antigen-presentation, cytokine, and adhesion pathways, and reduced macrophage- and CD45-positive cell signatures. Despite these sex-dependent transcriptional changes, LMNSC01 produced conserved protein changes in both sexes, reducing injury-associated ICAM-1 and restoring CX3CL1 proteins, proposing a novel molecular mechanism of LMNSCs modulating endothelial activation and neuron- microglia communication post injury. Our study provides further insight into sex differences in responses to injury and treatment after TBI and highlights candidate repair mechanisms, supporting further development of LMNSC01 as a minimally invasive therapy for TBI. This study provides evidence that a single intranasal dose of LMNSC01 can reprogram chronic neuroimmune and neurovascular dysfunction after TBI in both sexes. Despite distinct male and female injury and treatment responses, LMNSC01 produced a conserved reduction in ICAM-1 and increase in CX3CL1, suggesting reduced endothelial activation and restoration of homeostatic neuron-microglia signaling. Identification of shared changes in neurovascular and neuroimmune signaling provides a candidate mechanism for neural stem cell-mediated repair and supports the translational development of non-invasive intranasal LMNSC01 therapy for TBI.

title: 5-HT1A Antagonist WAY-100635 Prevents Chronic Neurodegeneration and Immune Activation After TBI.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) initiates secondary neurodegeneration that compromises interconnected neural circuits and contributes to persistent visual and neurobehavioral impairment. Pharmacological strategies that preserve vulnerable neurons and synapses while limiting chronic neuroinflammation remain an unmet therapeutic need. We previously identified the serotonin 1A receptor (5-HT1A) antagonist WAY-100635 through screening human stem cell-derived retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) and demonstrated that it promotes neuroprotection through cyclic adenosine monophosphate-dependent mitochondrial biogenesis. Here, we investigated whether post-injury treatment extends this neuroprotective efficacy to cerebral and visual circuitry following TBI. Male C57BL/6J mice aged 2-3 months underwent unilateral controlled cortical impact (CCI) involving the left visual cortex. Mice were randomly assigned to sham, untreated injury or treated injury groups, with 3-10 sham controls and 5-8 mice per injury group across experiments. WAY-100635 was administered intraperitoneally at 5 mg/kg daily, beginning 1 hour after injury and continuing for 6 weeks. Therapeutic efficacy was assessed using motor and psychological-health-relevant risk-taking/behavioral disinhibition by elevated-plus-maze assessment, visual electrophysiology, optokinetic responses, diffusion magnetic resonance imaging, and retinal and cortical histopathology. Unilateral cortical injury produced bilateral RGC dysfunction and loss, with greater degeneration in the eye contralateral to the injured hemisphere, consistent with predominantly crossed murine visual projections. WAY-100635 significantly preserved RGC survival and function, improved visual acuity and contrast sensitivity, and preserved visually evoked cortical responses to contralateral eye stimulation. Diffusion MRI revealed bilateral visual pathway abnormalities, with treatment selectively normalizing fractional anisotropy and radial kurtosis in the optic tract ipsilateral to cortical injury. In perilesional cortex, treatment preserved neuronal cell bodies and synapses detected by synaptophysin immunoreactivity while markedly reducing microglial/macrophage activation and reactive astrogliosis. These effects were accompanied by improved early motor performance and attenuation of injury-associated increases in open-arm exploration in the elevated plus maze. Cortical cavity volume was not significantly reduced, supporting preferential protection of vulnerable circuitry surrounding and connected to the primary lesion. These findings identify post-injury WAY-100635 treatment as a novel therapeutic intervention that combines neuronal and synaptic preservation with reduced chronic glial activation and improved functional outcomes. They support further translational development of serotonin 1A receptor antagonism to limit secondary neurodegeneration and the visual and neurobehavioral consequences of TBI.

title: Brainstem cholinergic cell loss causes slowly-developing motor impairments.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Pedunculopontine nucleus (PPN) cholinergic degeneration is a feature of Parkinson's disease (PD), but it is difficult to isolate the symptoms and circuit alterations caused by cholinergic cell loss in PD, where multiple nuclei are simultaneously degenerating. Here we develop a novel mouse model of brainstem cholinergic cell loss to define the timeline of symptom development and map physiological adaptations within the brainstem. Mild motor symptoms, including balance and motor learning deficits reminiscent of early-stage PD, developed after cholinergic lesion with an unexpected long delay. Ex vivo whole-cell recordings showed that cholinergic cell loss increased excitatory synaptic drive onto glutamatergic PPN neurons and increased their intrinsic ability to generate sustained action potential output. In parallel, fiber photometry experiments revealed a slight increase in glutamatergic sensory responsiveness that closely tracked the delayed onset of behavioral symptoms. Together, these results reveal that brainstem cholinergic cell loss triggers the reorganization of motor-related brainstem circuits, providing critical insight into the consequences of non-dopaminergic degeneration in PD.

title: Intrastriatal injection of amplified Lewy body dementia (LBD) fibrils in mice results in accumulation of fibrils with LBD structure and neurodegeneration.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: The defining neuropathologic feature of Lewy body dementia (LBD) and Parkinson's disease (PD) is alpha-synuclein (Asyn) fibril accumulation in Lewy bodies (LBs) and Lewy neurites (LNs). Recently, we developed a method to amplify Asyn fibrils derived from human post-mortem LBD brain tissue and determined that the structure of amplified Asyn fibrils is highly similar to the structure of fibrils directly isolated from LBD brain tissue. We examined whether injection of these fibrils into humanized Asyn mice recapitulates pathologic Asyn fibril accumulation with human LBD Asyn fibril structure. We utilized mice containing a null allele in the mouse Snca gene and a human SNCA transgene. Intrastriatal injection of amplified Asyn fibrils derived from 3 different LBD autopsy cases resulted in cytoplasmic and neuritic phospho-Asyn accumulation in the striatum, cortex, and amygdala bilaterally at 3mpi. Fibril injections produced a reduction in the number of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra, with LB-like inclusions in surviving neurons, and produced impaired sensorimotor function as measured on the accelerating rotarod test. Fibril accumulation increased 3.6-fold between 1 and 3 months post-injection (mpi) and was relatively stable between 3 and 5 mpi. We amplified fibrils from mouse brain tissue 5 mpi and collected single-particle cryo-EM data. High resolution 3D structural information could not be obtained because of the lack of helical twist, but comparison of the cryo-EM 2D class averages with those derived from amplified fibrils prepared from human LBD tissue revealed multiple matching classes, indicating that the Lewy fold is maintained in the fibrils that accumulate in mouse brain tissue. Our findings demonstrate an approach to model the accumulation of Asyn fibrils with LBD structure in mice, providing a platform for investigating disease mechanisms, imaging biomarkers, and therapeutics targeting Asyn in PD/LBD.

title: Clustering of the Adhesion-GPCR Latrophilin-3 Drives Excitatory Synapse Assembly.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Precise control of synapse formation is essential for brain function. Adhesion-GPCRs combine adhesion, signaling, and scaffold recruitment to regulate synapse formation, yet their mechanisms of action remain unclear. Here, we identify nanoscale clustering of the adhesion-GPCR Latrophilin-3 as a key mechanism regulating excitatory synapse assembly. We find that endogenous Latrophilin-3 forms densely packed nanoclusters, with larger nanoclusters enriched at excitatory synapses. To probe the functional significance of Latrophilin-3 clustering, we engineered an optogenetically controlled Latrophilin-3. Light-induced Latrophilin-3 clustering triggered robust excitatory synapse formation, which required both Latrophilin-3-mediated G-protein signaling and postsynaptic scaffold recruitment. Strikingly, clustering of a mutant Latrophilin-3 lacking known ligand-binding domains still promoted synapse formation, indicating that Latrophilin-3 ligands induce synapse assembly primarily by clustering Latrophilin-3. Our findings suggest a general paradigm by which extracellular ligand-induced clustering activates adhesion-GPCRs by generating compartmentalized signaling, which in the case of Latrophilin-3, cooperates with postsynaptic scaffold recruitment to drive synapse assembly.

title: Dog-human gene network colocalization links synaptic signalling and ubiquitination to compulsive disorders.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is highly polygenic, and the largest genome-wide association study (GWAS), with 53,660 cases and 2,044,417 controls, identified only 30 loci, a small fraction of loci estimated to explain its heritability - too few to resolve biological pathways 1 . Pet dogs develop a compulsive disorder (dogCD) similar to OCD 2 . In a GWAS of dogCD with 2,584 dogs from the community science project Darwin's Ark, each dog locus explains at least 40-fold more phenotypic variance than each human OCD locus, giving power equivalent to the human GWAS with 80-fold fewer individuals. Combining the two GWAS identifies a 165-gene network undetectable in humans at current sample sizes. This network is enriched for genes expressed in neurons, particularly in the amygdala and cortex, and comprises four biological processes: excitatory-inhibitory synaptic transmission, axon guidance and neuron recognition, protein ubiquitination, and adenylyl cyclase-activating G-protein-coupled receptor signaling. Like most complex human traits 3 , dogCD risk is likely driven by regulatory variation: fine-mapped dogCD SNPs are non-coding, and dogCD loci are enriched in candidate cis-regulatory elements (cCREs) in a new dog epigenomic atlas spanning eight brain regions. The cross-species network implicates an inherited risk architecture largely outside current OCD pharmacotherapy, and establishes pet dogs as a model for gene network discovery, particularly for conditions underpowered in human studies.

title: NE52-QQ57 attenuates post-ischemia protein phosphorylation in the mouse brain.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Cerebral ischemia induces a reduction in brain pH. GPR4, a proton-sensing G protein-coupled receptor is highly expressed in vascular endothelial cells. Pharmacological inhibition of GPR4 with NE52-QQ57 (NEQQ) reduces ischemia-induced blood-brain barrier (BBB) disruption and brain injury. To facilitate targeting GPR4 in vivo, it is important to better define the effect of NEQQ on post-ischemia signaling and the pharmacokinetics of NEQQ in vivo . We performed biochemical analysis following transient middle cerebral artery occlusion (tMCAO). We used Liquid Chromatography-Mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) to quantify the concentration of NEQQ in serum, brain, and peripheral tissues. NEQQ administration decreased the phosphorylation of PKA substrates, PKC substrates, ERK1/2, and CREB. LC-MS/MS analysis detected NEQQ in both ipsilateral and contralateral hemisphere of the brain at 5 h and 24 h after reperfusion, demonstrating that NEQQ crosses the BBB. In peripheral tissues, NEQQ exhibited highest level in kidney and lowest in the heart. In sham controls, average serum concentrations were ∼4 and 0.9 µg/g at 5 and 24 h, respectively. Following tMCAO, ipsilateral brain exhibited higher levels as compared to the contralateral side at 5 h while the difference diminished at 24 h. NEQQ attenuated the ischemia-induced activation of multiple signaling pathways. NEQQ exhibited broad distribution in peripheral organs, and its brain level was sufficient for GPR4 inhibition at 24 h after injection. These findings support the use of NEQQ as a pharmacological inhibitor of GPR4-mediated signaling following ischemic stroke.

title: A parsimonious, age-invariant, and psychometrically validated neural signature of task-control network functioning.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Neuroimaging has vast potential for identifying brain features that support individual and developmental differences in cognition, but challenges related to the dimensionality, unreliability, and unknown developmental properties of neuroimaging measures prevent this from being realized. We overcome these challenges by applying latent variable modeling to demand-related responses in the "task-control" frontoparietal and dorsal attention networks (FPN, DAN) within the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study and Human Connectome Project. Task-control activations are well-captured by a bifactor structure with a general factor spanning FPN/DAN and network-specific factors that is remarkably invariant across middle childhood to early adolescence and largely generalizes to adulthood. Trait-state-occasion modeling reveals a general task-control trait that shows robust associations with cognitive abilities, clinical symptoms, and grades. Repeated neuroimaging substantially increases associations. Findings establish a parsimonious neural signature that generalizes across samples, is stable across development, and has broad utility for understanding developmental and individual differences in goal-directed behavior.

title: Brainstem premotor circuits transform dental sensory input into coordinated jaw opening.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Protective actions require the rapid transformation of damage into coordinated activity of motor pools, yet the brainstem circuits implementing this operation remain poorly defined. Here, we use the tooth-trigeminal system to identify molecularly specified pathways linking intradental sensory input to opposing jaw motor pools. Optogenetic activation of tooth-associated sensory afferents evoked rapid, stimulus-locked jaw-opening. Intradental afferents formed functional monosynaptic connections with Pdyn+ neurons in the 5Sol transition zone and Calb2+ neurons in the 5Tr transition zone, identifying these regions as sensory-recipient premotor interfaces. Predominantly excitatory Pdyn+ 5Sol neurons provided monosynaptic input to anterior digastric motor neurons, whereas predominantly inhibitory Calb2+ 5Tr neurons provided bilateral monosynaptic input to masseter motor neurons. Activation of Pdyn+ 5Sol neurons was sufficient to evoke jaw opening. Together, these findings define complementary brainstem pathways positioned to couple jaw-opening drive with inhibition of antagonistic jaw-closing output, revealing a withdrawal-like sensorimotor computation adapted to cranial biomechanics.

title: Trigeminal Nerve Stimulation Attenuates Traumatic Brain Injury-Induced Neuronal Damage via CGRP-PINK1 Mitophagy Axis.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Secondary damage after traumatic brain injury (TBI) is driven by progressive mitochondrial failure, yet clinically viable strategies to directly safeguard mitochondrial networks remain a major therapeutic gap. Here, we show that non-invasive trigeminal nerve stimulation (TNS), which engages the brain's endogenous oxygen-conserving diving reflex, preserves neuronal survival by directly regulating the mitochondrial PINK1/Parkin quality-control pathway. We demonstrate that TBI induces the pathological aggregation of the outer mitochondrial membrane receptor TOM20, in a CGRP-dependent manner, which affects binding of the damage-sensor PINK1 and renders downstream Parkin-mediated rescue ineffective. TNS-induced neuronal CGRP release prevents this TOM20 aggregation, restoring proper PINK1 function and downstream Parkin activation. This preservation of mitochondrial architecture reinforces the outer membrane's barrier function, limiting pro-apoptotic cytochrome c leakage and supporting NRF2 antioxidant defenses, ultimately reducing progressive infarct expansion and recovering sensorimotor functions. The significance of this work lies in bridging physical neuromodulation directly to the preservation of organelle-level architecture. By demonstrating that stimulation of trigeminal afferents to recruit an oxygen-conserving reflex can stabilize outer membrane signaling architecture and preserve mitochondrial survival machinery, this study outlines a non-pharmacological strategy to protect mitochondrial function and inhibit acute post-traumatic neurodegeneration.

title: Nicotinic modulation of frontal circuits breaks the cycle of attentional performance failure.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: The ability to recover from consecutive failures is critical for adaptive behavior, yet the underlying neural mechanisms remain unclear. In vivo screening of neuromodulatory inputs onto frontal-sensory cognitive control circuit identified a frontal cholinergic mechanism that counteracts lapses in attentional engagement following repeated errors. Cholinergic input from the basal forebrain to the frontal cortex was necessary and sufficient to restore performance after errors, specifically after repeated-but not after a single-failure. This effect was mediated by α7-nicotinic acetylcholine receptors in frontal-sensory cortical neurons, which sustained cortical circuit activity and frontal-sensory cortical oscillations during attentional engagement. Targeted optogenetic activation of these frontal-sensory neurons disrupted cycles of attentional performance failure and reinstated behavioral performance in a mouse model of neuropsychiatric syndrome. These findings reveal a circuit-level mechanism of cholinergic control that confers cognitive resilience under conditions of persistent failure.
